item.title: Asteroid 2013 RX80 passes by
item.description:
10.10.2026, 10:50 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 668–1,493 m will pass Earth at 36.11 million km, or 93.9 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 25.8 km/s. For scale: an object of this scale is a heavyweight in the catalogue of near-Earth asteroids. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. The pass is entirely safe – approaches like this happen regularly and are tracked as a matter of routine.

Object record in the JPL database

This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. NASA classifies it as “potentially hazardous” – but that is purely a technical category for objects larger than about 140 m whose orbits come close to Earth's. No known object threatens us in the foreseeable future.

item.title: Southern Taurids meteor shower peak
item.description:
05.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

Few meteors, but an unusual share of fireballs – slow, very bright and worth the wait. At maximum, up to 5 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Taurus. A Moon 38% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Falcon 9 Block 5 | CHORUS
item.description:
31.12.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of Falcon 9 Block 5, operated by SpaceX. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: CHORUS is MDA's next generation Earth observation constellation, consisting of 2 radar satellites (C-band SAR and X-band SAR), in a 53.5 degree 600 km altitude LEO, with the X-band trailing the C-band by 60 minutes. A collaborative multi-sensor constellation, CHORUS will bring together diverse and unique imagery and data sources and provide a new level of near real-time insight and innovative Earth observation services. Operating in a unique mid-inclination orbit, CHORUS will be able to image day or night, regardless of weather conditions, with daily access of up to 95% of the coverage area. From an industry-leading 700km-wide imaging swath down to sub-metre high resolution, CHORUS will provide the most extensive and unrivalled Earth observation radar imaging capacity available on the market in a single mission. Launch dates slip often – check the current status before tuning into a webcast.

Mission details

item.title: Atlas V N22 | Starliner-1
item.description:
31.12.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of Atlas V N22, operated by United Launch Alliance. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: Starliner-1 is the first operational flight of a Starliner spacecraft to the International Space Station as part of NASA's Commercial Crew Program. Due to problems with the Starliner spacecraft's RCS attitude control system during the Crew Flight Test mission in 2024, this mission has been re-scoped to not carry a crew by NASA. It will instead deliver necessary cargo to the orbital laboratory and allow in-flight validation of the system upgrades implemented following the Crew Flight Test mission. item.title: Orionids meteor shower peak
item.description:
21.10.2027, 02:00 UTC

The year's second helping of dust from Halley's Comet, with fast, bright meteors. At maximum, up to 20 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Orion. Unfortunately the Moon will be 68% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

A Moon 56% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
